Big Sky was being slow on taking their handoffs, as usual, and when this aircraft got within one minute of the boundary - I turned them 90 degrees left and stopped them at a safe altitude for terrain. Big Sky Approach says they can wait until 2.5 miles away before taking the handoff - but for me I must turn an aircraft as to miss their airspace - unfortunately one minute was not enough time to turn the aircraft and they penetrated Big Sky Approach's airspace.This is a dangerous procedure without some sort of guarantee the hand off will be accepted - having aircraft descend below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) then having to turn them due to the refusal of Big Sky Approach to take handoffs in a timely manner is bad for safety and for expedition.I now know that one minute is not enough time to turn an aircraft and will therefore start turning aircraft two minutes from the boundary. Expect a surge in complaints from pilots and companies as it is exceedingly rare for a handoff to be taken by Big Sky that far out.
ASRS:1618650.s: The controller turned Aircraft X 90 degrees left during descent on the SADYL3 arrival to avoid terrain after Big Sky Approach delayed the handoff. The aircraft penetrated Big Sky airspace because one minute was insufficient for the turn, prompting the controller to initiate turns two minutes from the boundary in the future.

ASRS:1618651.n: Aircraft X landed 22L and exited the runway. Aircraft X advised LC1 they have hot brakes. Cab Coordinator and Controller in Charge made calls to roll the trucks. Aircraft Y was on the ILS 22R. Ground Control 1 advised there were trucks on 22R that were not in communication with ATC. Everyone made a blanket transmission to attempt to get a hold of the trucks. After several failed attempts Aircraft Y was told to go around.Not one of the trucks (maybe 5-6 of them) showed up on the ASDE-X. No primaries, nothing. If the visibility was low this most definitely would have resulted in an accident. The ASDE-X has been acting up for several months now, with an upcoming major construction project this needs to be fixed. Driver training to include local ATC. I don't know who teaches these driver classes but it might be a good idea to include ATC on it in some way.
ASRS:1618651.s: Aircraft Y executed a go-around on ILS 22R due to five to six unresponsive trucks on the runway that were not detected by the malfunctioning ASDE-X. The incident was caused by the trucks' lack of communication with ATC and the system's failure to display them, which the reporter attributes to equipment issues and insufficient driver training.

ASRS:1618659.n: Aircraft X was at 29,000 feet descending to 24,000 feet when I took the handoff. I don't remember him checking on. The pilot called me and asked me if I have traffic. I wasn't aware of any traffic, but either Conflict Alert went off, or I quick looked the sector above me. There was Aircraft Y at 28,000 feet wired with Aircraft X who was now at 28,000 feet descending to 24,000 feet. I told Aircraft X to turn 30 degrees right immediately and to expedite his descent. I didn't call and get control because I believed the situation was imminent and I had a Radar Assist who could have called. It was a Supervisor who was on my Assist and he's not good at all.There were a lot of conflict alerts going on during this entire session with military aircraft in or around my airspace. I was trying to suppress those Conflict Alerts to clean up the scope. I may have suppressed Aircraft X and Aircraft Y without knowing it. The sector above me was where the conflict happened. The controller working those aircraft is by far the worst controller I've ever worked with or around and that's not an exaggeration. That Controller needs to be taken off the boards. Bottom line or never let them work radar again.
ASRS:1618659.s: Air Traffic Controller X issued an immediate right turn and expedited descent to Aircraft X at 28,000 feet to avoid a conflict with Aircraft Y. The controller attributed the near-miss to suppressed Conflict Alerts and poor performance by the supervisor and the controller in the sector above.

ASRS:1618661.n: Aircraft X was on vectors for a GPS approach at MFR (this approach is to the airport not to the runway and not a precision approach). Aircraft X was issued distance from the final approach fix, heading 290 and 9000 feet until established. They read back direct and 9000 until established, which appeared would be essentially the same, so I did not correct them. Just south of the final approach fix the low altitude alert went off and I asked them to verify they had the terrain in sight. Initially they said no, but before I issued a low altitude alert they confirmed they had the terrain in sight. I issued the low altitude alert and gave the MVA (minimum vectoring altitude) of 8700 feet. They climbed to 8700 feet. I verified they were still established and re-cleared them for the approach.Tower should not advertise circling approaches due to terrain, most air carriers will not even accept this approach. Precision approaches should be used, unless visuals can be advertised due to terrain and complexity of the non-precision approaches. The airspace design does not allow precision approaches from the south.
ASRS:1618661.s: An air traffic controller issued a low altitude alert to Aircraft X during a GPS approach at MFR after the crew initially denied terrain visibility. The crew climbed to the minimum vectoring altitude of 8700 feet, confirmed terrain in sight, and were re-cleared for the approach.

ASRS:1618665.n: Aircraft on unexpected, uncoordinated arrival routing.Flight plan strip indicated Aircraft X to be on ZBW16/A90 LOA routing. Flight was not on that routing but going direct the fourth fix indicated in the LOA route. This was not coordinated as required.The amended routing had been entered into the flight plan, however a new flight plan strip was not generated by the amendment.Comply with the ZBW/A90 LOA or coordinated deviations verbally as required.Investigate if the ERAM (En Route Automation Modernization) automation performed correctly to verify if the required flight plan change was transmitted to the arriving sector.
ASRS:1618665.s: An aircraft arrived on an uncoordinated direct routing instead of the planned ZBW16/A90 LOA because the ERAM system failed to generate a new flight plan strip after an amendment. The reporter recommends verifying ERAM automation performance and ensuring future compliance with LOA or verbal coordination.

ASRS:1618667.n: Aircraft Y was cleared for takeoff with a suggested heading of 055 off of runway 25. I switched the aircraft when he started his right turn. Aircraft X was on final and I cleared him to land then I noticed Aircraft Y flying a 090 heading which made him a conflict with my aircraft on final. I told Aircraft X about the traffic and Aircraft X told me they were responding to a RA. I said roger and Aircraft X climbed to 1;400ft MSL and started it's descent to land.[I recommend we] change to Class Charlie airspace.
ASRS:1618667.s: An air traffic controller reported that Aircraft Y deviated from a cleared 055 heading to 090 after takeoff, creating a conflict with Aircraft X on final approach. Aircraft X responded to a Resolution Advisory by climbing to 1,400 feet MSL before descending to land.

ASRS:1618670.n: Aircraft X was on course west bound at 3,000 to stay out of the weather. The previous sector asked if I could work Aircraft X at 3,000 long before they were visible on my scope to which I answered affirmative. Approximately 30 minutes later I was alerted to a low altitude alert as Aircraft X entered a 3,400 MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude] at 3,000. I issued a low altitude alert and climbed Aircraft X to 3,400 immediately. There were many aircraft at 3,000 today due to winds and clouds at 3,500. I was already alert to other MVA's elsewhere in my airspace and after those aircraft passed the areas in question, I turned off my MVA map. I did not bring it back up upon receiving radar on Aircraft X. I will [make] a conscious effort to bring up my MVA map whenever aircraft are operating at or below 3,000 in the Macon/Columbus sectors.
ASRS:1618670.s: An air traffic controller failed to display the Minimum Vectoring Altitude map when Aircraft X entered the sector at 3,000 feet, triggering a low altitude alert as the aircraft descended below the 3,400-foot MVA. The controller immediately climbed the aircraft to 3,400 feet and attributed the incident to turning off the MVA map earlier and not reactivating it.

ASRS:1618674.n: I was merely the TMC (Traffic Management Coordinator) in the room when the event occurred. Aircraft X was inbound and lost his auto pilot. It appeared that the pilot was a little too panicked to fly the airplane on an instrument approach and was struggling to hold a heading and an altitude. A Controller was working the emergency at the time and by the Controller in Charge's (CIC) account, was doing a good job. The OM (Operations Manager) decided to send a Supervisor to take over the position, even though the Supervisor isn't certified at all on satellite sector. The CIC said that this caused a little chaos initially, but then it settled down. All of us in the room were scratching our heads as to why you'd pull a full time controller off the position to plug in a supervisor that controls 8 hours a month and isn't certified on the position and no, he isn't pilot either. Maybe this is a new FAA policy? If so, not a good one. As a part time controller myself, I would never want to take a position from a Controller on a position that I don't work and work an emergency. Staffing was not an issue and I can't fathom why the OM would put the supervisor in that position and why the pilot didn't get the more experienced person available. My recommendation would be to let the controller do their job.
ASRS:1618674.s: A TMC reported that during an emergency involving Aircraft X's autopilot failure, an Operations Manager replaced a competent controller with an uncertified Supervisor. The reporter stated this caused initial chaos and questioned the decision to remove an experienced controller from the position.

ASRS:1618679.n: I received a briefing to take over the sector. The last part of the briefing was that the current controller had not issued traffic to Aircraft Y at 33,000 feet and Aircraft X descending to 24,000 feet and was already below 35,000 feet. Right away, my first clearances as I took over were issuing traffic to both aircraft. Both aircraft came back and said they had TCAS resolutions. Aircraft Y was observed at 32,700 feet and Aircraft X climbed back to 35,000 feet. I do not recall that the targets ever merged. After traffic passed, I cleared Aircraft X to descend. After I transferred radio communications of Aircraft X to the next sector that sector controller advised me that Aircraft X reported moderate turbulence at 24,000 feet. Shortly after, the receiving sector controller was heard coordinating injuries encountered on Aircraft X due to the moderate turbulence. This was the first report of moderate turbulence I had heard. The sector also said that the pilot of Aircraft X made mention of an engine configuration due to the TCAS response. There was no mention of any of this from Aircraft X on my frequency.In my briefing, I was told that there was light chop between 24,000 and 26,000 feet and maybe up to 28,000 feet. This was consistent with the reports I was getting during my previous session at this sector about 40 minutes earlier. During that earlier session, I had solicited and received numerous reports of light chop between 24,000 and 26,000 feet from aircraft climbing westbound. There were no reports from the aircraft climbing out eastbound. I did not get any reports of any chop from any aircraft in the area that Aircraft X was traversing. Aircraft X checked on my frequency descending to 24,000 feet 2 to 3 minutes after responding to a TCAS RA with no loss of separation on the previous frequency. Upon leveling at 24,000 feet Aircraft X reported moderate turbulence to which I responded expect lower shortly as the aircraft was still in the previous sectors airspace. There had been no other reports in this area worse than light chop previously. The aircraft was descended upon entering my airspace and then two minutes later they came back requesting priority handling due to an injury in the back of the aircraft. I asked if they needed any assistance or were declaring a medical emergency to which they responded negative. A couple minutes after that they reported two crew members injured in the back of the aircraft, one with serious injuries. After coordinating everything they were requesting at the airport I asked the aircraft if they experienced turbulence worse than the moderate they reported. They replied that it was just moderate however responded to the RA that had just completed prior to checking on my frequency resulted in an engine not being configured properly.There were no preceding arrivals on their flight path and previous PIREPs solicited from departures in the same area reported nothing worse than continuous light chop. All AIRMETs and SIGMETs were broadcasted for forecasted chop and real world PIREPs were received. Solicited ride reports from multiple surrounding sectors had been nothing worse than light to moderate chop for the area with nothing indicating that injuries could be a possibility. We are thinking that because of the RA climb while rapidly descending to meet a crossing restriction and subsequent high rate of descent after clearing the conflict put the aircraft in an undesirable condition with a higher than normal airspeed into the light chop. It was clear the aircraft was placed in an unstabilized descent due to the RA and interrupted decent profile. If the restriction was to be tight afterwards and as the aircraft stated one engine wasn't speed configured properly the aircraft could have asked for relief from the restriction. The aircraft went from high descent rate to leveling at the crossing restriction point which wasn't in my airspace for further decent yet.
ASRS:1618679.s: An air traffic controller took over a sector where Aircraft X and Y experienced a TCAS resolution, causing Aircraft X to enter an unstabilized descent with an improperly configured engine. Upon leveling at 24,000 feet, Aircraft X encountered moderate turbulence, resulting in two crew injuries, which the controller attributed to the high airspeed from the TCAS-induced descent profile.

ASRS:1618695.n: On downwind to XXR, cleared for visual, I set 2800 feet. Captain verified it. On base leg, we were told of a King Air on the opposite side. We saw it on TCAS. I'd planned and briefed joining final outside FAF, as we were still descending to GSIA (Glide Slope Intercept Altitude). As I turned to base, about 3 miles outside FAF, I looked left to see the runway and adjusted the heading bug slightly to left for better intercept angle, or so I thought. All of a sudden, the sight picture looked lower, I looked up and the aircraft was at 2100-2200 feet MSL. I looked at the alerter and it was set to 1500 feet. Clicked autopilot off, climbed back up to 2800 feet MSL. At this time, ATC gave us a low altitude alert. We acknowledged, and at 2800 MSL, intercepted glideslope and continued on approach to landing. I think I may have inadvertently twisted the altitude alerter instead of heading bug to the left as I was setting a better intercept angle. But because the visual picture looked low, I was able to recognize and correct the situation.
ASRS:1618695.s: The pilot inadvertently set the altitude alerter to 1500 feet instead of adjusting the heading bug while descending on base leg, causing an unintended descent to 2100 feet. The pilot recognized the error, disengaged the autopilot, and climbed back to 2800 feet after receiving a low altitude alert from ATC.

ASRS:1618704.n: Behind schedule flight into BUR. On final descent, we requested the RNAV VISUAL 33, told to expect and briefed it. While being vectored by Final Approach Controller, he asked if we could do the ILS 8 circle to 15. We accepted.We were vectored on the ILS very close to the marker and high and fast. We got visual contact with the airport and began circling to 15. We were fast and high from the beginning. The Captain configured for a flaps 40 landing and circled to 15. We had briefed an obstacle near the final approach course for 15 (a Tower) and kept a close eye on that. We began to pick up a tailwind on base leg while being somewhat high on visual glidepath. We received several 'Don't Sink' call outs and the Captain said correcting. On short final, we received a 'Pull Up', but being so close to landing we continued and landed. We should have gone around. We arrived into ZZZ about 20 minutes late due to minor maintenance issue [earlier]. Upon arrival we received weather packet and reviewed. Burbank TAF was within visibility and wind limits, though it was forecast to go out after our arrival. The Agent came down and told us Dispatch had locked out the flight and to call them. I did, and was told Burbank was forecast to go out of wind with an amended TAF that had just come out. METAR winds were still 080/6 but all winds in TAF were out of limits for a Runway 8 arrival. We needed 5000-5 for charted visuals to 15 and 33 and it was below that. It was above 100-3 which allowed for a circle off of ILS to 8. I checked BUR airport pages and reviewed circling approaches with FO (First Officer) to see if this would be legal and advisable. I called the Chief in Operations and he said they were recommending ILS 8 circle to Dispatch and an option. Dispatch called back and we agreed that we could legally depart with present weather and forecast and we did.We monitored wind on METAR enroute to BUR. Normal operations with me as PF (Pilot Flying) and I briefed ILS to visual to Runway 8 as current ATIS and landing data allowed arrival to it. I also briefed that we would do charted visuals if new weather allowed and winds swapped out. I noted we would circle if we had to as we had discussed in ZZZ. When new ATIS was available, FO pulled it up and winds did not allow landing on Runway 8, but 15 and 33 were within landing limits. This eliminated Runway 8 but visibility and ceiling had improved to allow charted RNAV visuals. Since we were dealing with almost a direct crosswind, and we were on arrival that ended near the initial fix for the 33 RNAV visual, I preferred that approach. It had a slight tailwind on 33 but stopping margins were around 1000 feet. I loaded 33 visual into the box and FO requested it with SoCal Approach, and he took us off arrival and vectored us toward the first fix of RNAV visual to 33. Abeam Van Nuys and at 5000 feet in IMC, he said turn left heading 040 and join the localizer to 8. We queried and he said expect the circle to 15 off ILS to Runway 8. We turned and intercepted and were full deflection high and IMC. We asked for lower and he gave us 3000 feet. We broke out just outside BUDDE and I told FO I had field and to call it visual. He noted we were high on GS and I said we are circling and we can get down. He was clearly in Yellow and headed to Red. I was ok as we were mid-field downwind visual with gear out and configuring. As we turned base, the tailwind started to increase our ground speed and I had to increase bank angle to 30 degrees, went over 30 as the turbulence started increasing. My plan, which I verbalized was to make a very shallow turn to final and let the strong crosswind line me up at 1000 feet with runway centerline, I was effectively wings level on base to final fully configured. Our ground speed was very high with the quartering tailwind on base and I was having a hard time staying spooled within speed and not sinking excessively. I was in Yellow and headed to Red. We were going to sink above the recommended rate of 1000 feet but it was getting hard to keep the touchdown target on the nose and maintain speed. The wind did not abate and I am not sure of final altitude but we lined up on centerline very close to 500 feet and received a SINK RATE cautionary GPWS. I noted it, and as I turned into wind, I was of the belief that rate would stabilize as GS bled off. It did not due to gusts and turbulence rolling off building to east of runway. Rate again triggered SINK RATE a few times on final and I added power but did not want to raise nose and put my touchdown point down the runway. After clearing airport boundary fence we received a GPWS warning PULL UP. At that point I was flaps 40 in moderate rolling turbulence with power back and flight path on 1000 foot marker. I landed as I felt it was best and safest choice given altitude and conditions. We were able to exit mid-field, and upon arrival I called Operations and told them that circling to 15 from 8 was not recommended, and that given winds and tailwinds on base a high sink rate was necessary to maintain glide path. I stated that charted visuals to 15 should be requested.
ASRS:1618704.s: The crew, operating a delayed flight into Burbank, accepted an ATC vector for an ILS 8 circle to Runway 15 but encountered high speed, tailwinds, and turbulence. Despite multiple GPWS warnings, the Pilot Flying continued the approach and landed, later reporting that a go-around was necessary due to the unstable conditions.

ASRS:1618719.n: After downloading and executing the [weight and balance] data, we received an FMC message 'UNABLE 280 KTS AT CHURO.' We discovered the cause to be the Cost Index of 20 set by the Dispatch release which commands a 261 knot descent after transition from mach. We had to spend time finding out the cause which is not optimal during the very busy time after [weight and balance] takeoff data arrives. As we all know, the moment the [weight and balance] takeoff data arrives is one of the busiest times of a flight so this is not inconsequential. This happened again on our very next flight as well, however this time we quickly discovered it was due to the same thing. The CI (Cost Index) set to below 40 is obviously to save fuel and accomplish our third operational priority of efficiency. But since this programming generates an airspeed that does not comply with a published STAR, it becomes a clear safety issue, greatly increasing the likelihood of pilot violations/deviations if the programming is not corrected. This policy therefore places our number one policy priority, Safety, below our third priority, efficiency.The variable cost index is a great tool for saving fuel, however it cannot be one-size-fits-all. It must be applied at the appropriate time and only where its use does not generate a conflict with the planned STAR at the arrival airport. Crews should not be expected to load an arrival that generates errors and subsequently have to rely on other RRM (Risk and Resource Management) blocks to then correct the planned input that caused the error. We should plan for success and not failure. The use of CI less than 40 should be carefully selected by the Dispatcher at airports where the planned STAR has no airspeed restrictions. However, we can take advantage of the variable cost index to save fuel if used properly. In the case where the airspeed restrictions are 280 knots, a cost index of 36 generates a perfect 280 knot transition. We can take advantage of the lower cost index and still comply with the speed requirements. Interestingly, all ZZZ STARS have a magenta box dictating a 280 knot transition. Why not use CI36 all the time on ZZZ arrivals? This puts us in compliance with this requirement the instant we load our [weight and balance] data at the gate. It requires no further action by the pilot, as opposed to now where we must modify the VNAV descent page to comply. This is setting up for success not failure. On STARS where there is a 270 knot restriction, a CI of 28 generates a 271 knot transition, which is the closest you get to 270 knots without getting slower. Again, we obtain the lower CI fuel savings and avoid having to reprogram our VNAV Descent page. It would take a little time to build the database to check on airspeed requirements for the different STARS, but this should be simple programming. Simply put, 'IF STAR=XXXXX, THEN CI MUST BE GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO 36'. Then repeat for the others in our system. Used smartly, this could be a great tool for saving fuel, but as we can see, blindly applying a lower CI is setting our crews up for likely violations and deviations and misplacing our operational priorities.
ASRS:1618719.s: Pilots reported that a Dispatch-set Cost Index of 20 caused FMC "UNABLE 280 KTS" errors during the pre-flight weight and balance data load for arrivals with 280-knot STAR restrictions. The crew identified this conflict between fuel-saving programming and published speed limits as a safety issue that forces manual VNAV corrections and increases the risk of pilot deviations.

ASRS:1618751.n: Cleared for the OHSEA 1 RNAV arrival for RWY 20R, with visual approaches in use. Crew elected to load the RNAV Z 20R approach for vertical and lateral reference, but later executed an ILS to 20R due to deteriorating weather conditions at the field.First Issue:During preflight planning, crew determined using the LAX 127 degree radial and ELB 227 degree radial in FIX pages 1 and 2 to reference the LAX Class B airspace structure (LAX 10-1B in SNA reference pages). Crew noted that the way point constraints on the RNAV RNP Z RWY 20R (SNA 12-21) for MNNIE and KLIPP were 210 knots or less, which matches the depiction on the approach plate (Ball note 1:210 knots maximum at MNNIE and KLIPP). However, using the fix pages above, the crew determined that both these points are under the LAX Class B airspace, and therefore under FAR 91.117, the maximum speed for these points is 200 knots.As recommended in Departure Arrival note 2, crew placed a hard speed constraint of 200 knots at LAXBB, and changed the speed constraints at MNNIE and KLIPP to 200B (less than 200 knots) to comply with FAR 91.117. However, it is extremely disconcerting that the approach plates and the database is coded to allow for a direct violation of FAR 91.117, and that direct manual intervention is required preclude a violation of FAR's.Second Issue:During the descent phase of the flight, flight was on profile and speed with LNAV and VNAV Path. Passing SIPPP intersection, ATC directed 'After TANDY, proceed direct to KAYNN and descend via the remainder of the OHSEA 1 arrival.' Crew complied with modifying the legs page, and after TANDY, the FMS vertical path showed a sudden and considerable deviation above path. The pilot flying immediately engaged full speed brakes with idle thrust, which resulted in a 2600 FPM descent rate. Passing 11,000 ft MSL, PF (Pilot Flying) began to shallow the descent rate to get below 250 knots at 10,000 feet, and directed the PM (Pilot Monitoring) to advise ATC that we would not be able to comply with the KAYNN restriction due to the shortcut. The Controller directed the flight to 'Maintain the current rate of descent to cross KAYNN at 7,000 feet', with the obvious implication that ATC didn't care about the speed but the altitude. The crew interjected that we were unable to exceed the maximum speed limits below 10,000 and below the LAX Class B airspace. The Controller soon switched the flight to another sector, with the discrepancies never being addressed. While the above issue regarding the published arrival was disconcerting, this Captain finds the apparent disregard of this Controller for FAR 91.117 absolutely alarming. This Controller clearly has no idea that the laws of physics are not negotiable, and that what he was asking this crew to do, in the time and space allotted, was simply not possible while remaining in compliance with basic FAR restrictions, and when the crew voiced their concerns, the Controller was unwilling to even acknowledge their concerns.The next time this Captain encounters these kind of ATC directions, he will be more directive and state in explicit terms: Unable to comply. I acted as FO (First Officer) and PM (Pilot Monitoring) flying routing to SNA. While executing a clearance to descend via RDHOT.OHSEA1, SoCal Approach instructed us to proceed direct from TANDY to KAYNN, a routing that passed through Class B airspace. During the descent to be at or below 7,000 MSL at KAYNN, the PF (Pilot Flying) began to slow to 250 KIAS to comply with the airspeed restriction below 10,000 MSL. While slowing, SoCal Approach instructed us to maintain our current rate of descent of approximately 2,500 FPM. Facing the 250 KIAS speed restriction followed by a 200 KIAS maximum speed restriction once we descended below the 7,000 MSL floor of Class B airspace enroute to complying with a 5,000 MSL required altitude at LAXBB, maintaining 2,500 FPM wasn't possible. When we notified SoCal Approach, the Controller responded saying that he required that rate of descent. We responded saying that we would descend as quickly as we could while complying with the speed restrictions.Further complicating the situation is the fact that the RNAV Z Rwy 20R approach has #1 ball notes associated with the fixes MNNIE and KLIPP that state 'MAX 210 KIAS'. The B737 FMC (Flight Management Computer) has these speeds associated with that approach as well, which could easily cause crews to fly faster than the 200 KIAS speed restriction below Class B airspace.
ASRS:1618751.s: A B737 crew descending via the OHSEA 1 arrival to SNA reported that ATC issued a direct routing and descent rate conflicting with FAR 91.117 speed limits in LAX Class B airspace. The crew noted that approach database speed constraints of 210 knots also violated the 200-knot restriction, requiring manual intervention to remain compliant.

ASRS:1618754.n: After parking brake set at gate, aircraft continued to move forward very slowly as englines [were shutting down] with ince on ramp. Parking brake was set with good pressure. Aircraft moved forward approximately 3 feet. Most likely cause of movement was ice of ramp and residual thrust from engines as they spooled down. After taxi in, the Captain followed the Marshaller's command to stop the aircraft. Captain set the parking brake. However, before the engines were shut down, we noticed a very slight aircraft movement forward. We shut down the engines which arrested the movement. We think we slid approximately 3 feet forward with the park brake set.
ASRS:1618754.s: The Captain reported that after setting the parking brake at the gate, the aircraft slid approximately 3 feet forward on an icy ramp due to residual engine thrust during shutdown. The movement ceased once the engines were shut down.

ASRS:1618757.n: After F/O (First Officer) finished the walk around he said he had taken a picture of something that was being loaded onto the aircraft and asked if I had ever seen this before. It looked like a small trash can on a small pallet, wrapped in plastic. He said it was labeled 'cryogenic medical supplies'. Preliminary DG (Dangerous Goods) report had said no DG on this flight. I went down to the ramp to see what this was. There were 3 of these containers each was marked 'cryogenic'. Dispatcher was called. He talked to Load Planner, neither had any record of DG to be loaded. Called [Station] Operations, they called back and said there was no paperwork on these containers, therefore, they were being removed from the aircraft. I went downstairs to the ramp, talked to the Ramp Supervisor and saw that they had been removed. F/O should be commended for his diligence. If he hadn't taken that picture I would have never known. During the exterior aircraft inspection I noticed some strange cargo that appeared to be 3 barrels of medical equipment with dry ice. I took a photo of it and showed it to the Captain. At that moment we also got an ACARS message that said No Dangerous Goods. The CA (Captain) called and [Station] Operations. They said no Hazmat planned. The CA went out on the ramp and saw that the possible Hazmat cargo was loaded. The CA then called Operations again about the cargo, after a few minutes they said the cargo in question was removed from the aircraft. The rest of the flight was normal.
ASRS:1618757.s: The First Officer and Captain identified three unlabeled cryogenic medical containers on the ramp during pre-flight, despite ACARS and paperwork indicating no dangerous goods. Operations confirmed the error and removed the cargo before departure, preventing an unauthorized hazardous materials load.

ASRS:1618760.n: In EUG using no Tower communications due to early morning the Tower was not open. Got ATC clearance from Center, void if not off by XA:57. We were rolling down the runway with XA:57 on the UTC clock. ATC starts to call us saying they haven't heard from us and we are passed our void time. I look down at the clock and it still says XA:57. We lifted off and the aircraft clock still showed XA:57. My question is if we are told a clearance is void if not off by XA:57, does that mean we have to be airborne by XA:56 or is it like I think XA:57? To me it would be the clock showing XA:58, that would be the void time. Also our clocks don't show the time in seconds so starting a takeoff with the clock showing us right at the minute before our clearance voids seems appropriateOur clocks are synced to GPS so I think they are accurate. I obviously wasn't going to high speed abort a takeoff due to ATC calling me saying my clearance was void, but it was distracting. We were transmitting on UNICOM but monitoring Seattle center on takeoff. Also I am certain my clock still showed XA:57 at liftoff so why does ACARS show XA:58. Does ACARS round up?
ASRS:1618760.s: The pilot departed EUG without Tower communications, receiving a Center clearance void if not off by 05:57 UTC. Although ATC called stating the clearance was void, the pilot noted the aircraft clock still read 05:57 at liftoff, raising questions about whether the void time applies at the start or end of the minute.

ASRS:1618775.n: The recent change in the flight attendant assignments on the B767 has created an unsafe condition in the cabin. With the removal of the flight attendant in the B zone galley, there is no longer a crew member in position when the pilots need to utilize the restrooms at doors 2 left and right. In the past it was common practice to have a restroom locked off prior to the pilots walking through business class to use them, so that the pilots would not have to wait in line for a restroom. Now this is no longer possible which exposes the flight crew to possible unhappy passengers as we now need to cut in line in front of them. There is no longer an available cabin crew member being present in the immediate area in the event of a conflict or safety issue between pilot and passenger should one occur.Additionally, there is no longer a flight attendant in position to assist a pilot utilizing the crew rest facility at seat 7d should a safety issue occur. Passengers are now free to loiter in the b zone galley area, just steps away from the rest facility at seat 7d. This creates an unsafe condition in that the flight crew member sitting in seat 7D would have no warning or assistance against any unsavory passengers that are now free to assemble in the mid galley area to plan a hostile attack against them. As an LCA (Line Check Airman), I am constantly utilizing seat 6d for my crew rest due to double augmentation of the cockpit crew. This seat is easy to view from the mid galley area and would be easy to reach in less than a second should a hostile force decide to attack. Additionally, pilots are now completely alone while they use the restroom in that area, in the low light condition of cruise flight. Passengers from the aft cabin are already utilizing these restrooms unchallenged, posing and additional safety risk.Not to mention the reduction in service we now will offer to our Business customers, the people we need to please the most.A flight crew safety issue [has been created] on the B767 by removing a cabin crew member from this area, and this should be corrected immediately.
ASRS:1618775.s: A Line Check Airman reported that removing a flight attendant from the B767's B-zone galley created an unsafe condition during cruise. This change leaves pilots vulnerable to passenger conflict while using restrooms or the crew rest facility at seat 7D due to a lack of immediate cabin crew support.

ASRS:1618791.n: (Lithium Battery) [loaded by cargo warehouse] without a booking. [Other item] was also [loaded] by [cargo warehouse] without a cargo booking.
ASRS:1618791.s: The cargo warehouse loaded a lithium battery and another item onto the aircraft without a booking. No specific aircraft, phase of flight, or outcome was described in the narrative.

ASRS:1618807.n: This is not the first time this has happened. We had a lateral deviation [prior to this event] and filed an [ASRS Report]. Fortunately this happened at cruise. FMS (Flight Management) # 2 dropped offline during cruise. Messages on the FMS included: Single Operation, flight plan drops off, Independent Mode, ACARS (Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System) not INIT, ACARS does not work on both FMS's, Lateral Mode is also lost on FMS # 2.On this particular flight there was no deviations but I'm filling out this [ASRS Report] to bring attention to all concerned that this is becoming a problem with FMS # 2 just dropping offline for no apparent reason. This has become more frequent since updating a software on the FMS which now requires us to put in the landing airport, OAT (Outside Air Temperature) and Altimeter setting to get landing aero data.Look into the software update to the FMS to find out what is causing the FMS to go into single mode and especially why the flight plan drops off. A similar incident happen again [recently] and I will be filling out another report.
ASRS:1618807.s: Pilots reported that FMS #2 dropped offline during cruise, causing loss of lateral mode and flight plan data. They attributed the recurring issue to a recent software update requiring manual entry of landing airport, OAT, and altimeter settings.

ASRS:1618841.n: The First Officer/Pilot Monitoring noticed the turn coordinator was unstable and was giving us incorrect indications. After observing erratic indications and taking into consideration the weather that was at our destination, we decided to return to ZZZ. We were VMC and we were halfway to ZZZ1 when the decision to turn back was made. The weather in ZZZ1 was low visibility and so we elected to turn back and remain in VMC. We contacted ATC and got a clearance back to ZZZ. We ended up cancelling a few minutes later. Then, we let [Operations Control] know what the issue and plan was.
ASRS:1618841.s: The First Officer noticed an unstable turn coordinator giving incorrect indications while en route to ZZZ1 in VMC. The crew returned to ZZZ to avoid low visibility at the destination, obtained an ATC clearance, and subsequently cancelled the flight.

ASRS:1618851.n: During cruise, approximately 30 minutes from landing in ZZZ after a routine flight, First Officer mentioned he didn't feel well. Then, he lost consciousness for 30-60 seconds. Captain (Pilot Flying) got a Flight Attendant to the cockpit, [advised ATC] and informed Dispatch. First Officer recovered and was met on landing by first responders and walked to an exam area and then an ambulance. Captain accompanied First Officer to hospital.
ASRS:1618851.s: During cruise, the First Officer lost consciousness for 30-60 seconds while the Captain was flying. The Captain diverted attention to get a Flight Attendant, advised ATC, and landed, where the First Officer was met by first responders and taken to a hospital.

ASRS:1618854.n: About 15 minutes after departure [and] climbing though 17,000 feet, we experienced a sudden jolt which we believe was the result of the wake from another aircraft. There was no TCAS indication of the other aircraft. We told ATC and they said a heavy B777 was 13 miles from us. We saw nothing on TCAS after scrolling up, down and changing range. I spoke with the flight attendants. [One of the flight attendants] said she hit her knee on a cart. No other passengers were up nor were there any complaints from any of the passengers. The seat belt sign remained on for the duration of the flight.Vectored too close to a heavy aircraft. We could not see the other aircraft nor [did we have] any TCAS indication. ATC just said 'caution wake turbulence' and stated he was about 13 miles from us. They could [have] suggested a heading change since we were climbing on assigned heading and altitude. It was impossible for me to know where the other aircraft was, so I could not take any action to avoid the wake turbulence. During climb out, flight crew was advised of heavy B777 traffic that was outside visual range with 'caution wake turbulence' included. Flight was unable to find traffic either visually or on TCAS displays. Attempts were made to get updates on location of traffic. ATC reported traffic outside of thirteen miles. Workload was very high on flight deck with strong tailwinds accelerating the need to quickly prepare for the arrival into [destination airport]. It had been several minutes since the first report of the traffic when the flight experienced no more than two seconds of very strong turbulence which quickly stopped and the flight resumed flight in calm smooth air. Communication with the cabin was established to ascertain the status of cabin crew and passengers. One Flight Attendant reported a possible injury to the knee. Captain advised her to stay seated for the duration of the flight. Flight arrived [at destination] without further event. ATC did a poor job of traffic separation. The flight crew was task loaded and unable to visually acquire high altitude and high speed traffic on what were apparently intersecting flight paths in time to prevent an encounter with strong wake turbulence. ATC needs to do more than just give 'caution wake turbulence' advisories at high altitude and high airspeed situations. The flight crew was in a high task load situation and had very little opportunity to spot traffic that was outside visual range.
ASRS:1618854.s: During climb through 17,000 feet, the flight crew encountered strong wake turbulence from a B777 reported 13 miles away by ATC, despite no TCAS or visual contact. The event caused a flight attendant knee injury, which the reporter attributed to poor ATC separation and insufficient traffic advisories during high workload.

ASRS:1618860.n: Hazardous liquid spilled in forward cargo department.Cause: TSA missed bag with hazardous liquid in checked bag contained in laundry detergent containers.
ASRS:1618860.s: A hazardous liquid spilled in the forward cargo hold after the TSA failed to detect a bag containing the liquid in laundry detergent containers within checked baggage.

ASRS:1618861.n: Windy and snowy night at ZZZ. Boarded passengers and closed door. Got deiced and anti-iced at gate. Deicers couldn't deice our radome since the deicing truck couldn't get to the front of the aircraft. Deicer said they'd finish the deicing [and] spray the radome upon our push into the alley. We called for push. Ramp Tower cleared us to push. To the best of my knowledge, the Ramp Controller's exact words were, ''Cleared to push.'' The clearance was without qualification or further detail. Simply, 'Cleared to push.' I repeated same to our ground crew. We got pushed into the snowy alley. After resetting brakes, I asked ground crew to stay on interphone for a moment until I could re-establish radio contact with deicer (that is, so as to ask him if he needed engines off for the radome deicing). I believe the deicer's reply was that it didn't matter.I then cleared our ground crew to disconnect interphone, got pin and salute, etc. We started engines and deicer deiced our radome. Upon receipt of deicer's final report, and ground crew now gone, I was now able to toggle up Comm 2 audio (Ramp Tower). Our aircraft status was: stationary, parking brake parked, both engines running, and deicing and anti-icing fully completed. About the first thing I heard over Comm 2 was someone talking about having hit something.I initially thought it was a deicing truck (not ours, of course) somewhere out on the ramp that was discussing having hit something, but it turned out that there was now a [Company] 737 off our right wing - at our 3:30 position. He was telling us that as he had been taxiing forward (from a position behind us), the leading edge of his left wingtip (winglet) had contacted the aft edge of the winglet on our right wingtip.We remained parked - did not move - and called for [Company] Aircraft Maintenance to come out and inspect us. They came out and confirmed the aforementioned contact and confirmed some visible damage - but also said that our current state was safe: ''OK to get tugged back to the gate.'' We called for a tug and crew to tug us back to a gate. Due to the 28-knot winds gently buffeting our aircraft, we had not been aware of wingtip contact. There had been no jolt or bump perceptible to us (or, if there was a slight bump or jolt, it had been disguised by the wind.). Normal deplaning of passengers.
ASRS:1618861.s: A Company 737 taxiing behind a stationary, deicing 737 at ZZZ contacted the parked aircraft's right winglet with its left winglet. The collision went unnoticed by the parked crew due to 28-knot winds masking the impact, though maintenance confirmed visible damage and cleared the aircraft to be tugged back to the gate.

ASRS:1618870.n: The new Flight Attendant requirement to arrive at the airport is one hour and fifteen minutes prior to departure. Pilot requirement has not changed, and is still one hour. The problem is that in most cases pilots and flight attendants take the same transportation to the airport from the hotel. This raises several issues. One is that FAR 117 rest requirement and on duty times are no longer accurate for pilots. On some occasions, legalities for pilots to continue a sequence come down to the minute, and I don't believe those computations are accurate if the assumed arrival time at the airport is one hour, when management is requiring pilots to be there with the flight attendants an hour and fifteen minutes prior.This is exacerbated by some stations that excessively pad departure times from the hotel. SBGR is a chronic problem. On this flight, we arrived at the airport about 40 minutes prior to required sign-in for pilots. How should FAR 117 be computed in this case? The stated reason for SBGR to excessively pad the pickup time for crewmembers is that on occasion traffic can be bad. In 19 years of flying to SBGR, I've been late to the airport once. And when we arrived at the gate on that particular day, the airplane took another 45 minutes past departure time to arrive at the gate. There is a reasonable standard to be applied, and I don't believe what is happening is either FAR 117 legal, contractually appropriate or justified, and much less reasonable. At a minimum, pilots should not be subject to the contractual requirement of a different employee group.SBGR management and the Company do not comply with FAR 117 requirements. Suggest separate pilot transportation to the airport, and more reasonable pickup times.
ASRS:1618870.s: A pilot reported that SBGR management's excessive padding of crew transportation times forces pilots to arrive 40 minutes early, conflicting with FAR 117 rest and duty time calculations. The pilot concluded this practice is legally non-compliant and requested separate pilot transportation with reasonable pickup times.

ASRS:1618895.n: L ENGINE FUEL FILTER EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System) MESSAGE CAME ON DURING CLIMB. EICAS MESSAGE CAME ON AND OFF SEVERAL TIMES AND REMAINED ON THROUGHOUT MOST OFF THE FLIGHT. LEFT ENGINE VIBRATED AND VIBRATION INCREASED DURING DESCENT COMPLIED WITH NON-NORMAL AND NORMAL CHECKLISTS [REQUESTED PRIORITY HANDLING] AND RETURNED TO ZZZZ. (Out of maintenance log.)We did not want to proceed over water with a possibility of fuel contamination. I was the monitoring pilot and completed the non-normal and normal checklists while FO (First Officer) was flying and handling ATC, I assumed the controls for the landing. We returned safely to ZZZZ. Excellent assistance from my FO.System malfunction.
ASRS:1618895.s: The monitoring pilot and First Officer experienced a left engine fuel filter EICAS message and increased vibration during climb and descent. They returned safely to ZZZZ due to suspected fuel contamination, attributing the event to a system malfunction.

ASRS:1618903.n: Where to start. The release did not put NOTAMS for MYAM in the release so we did not know about MYAM changing its name. A Tower, with ATIS, Ground and Tower frequencies have been built and opened. So we did not call Tower 20 miles out, it is now a part time Class D airspace. ARFF has been reduced so not sure if it is enough for our size aircraft. On Unicom frequency Tower called us to call on Tower frequency. We called and were told cleared to land. We called Ground Control and taxied in. They are still in training and cannot coordinate IFR departures. Center did not hand us off to Tower either and had us cancel IFR and squawk VFR. The NOTAMs did not populate in the release. Jeppesen charts are not updated for the change of Class airspace and frequencies. The Company page is also outdated now. Tower said they have been open 2 weeks.
ASRS:1618903.s: The flight crew arrived at MYAM unaware of its new Class D status due to missing NOTAMs and outdated charts. Center canceled their IFR flight plan, and they landed after Tower contact, noting uncoordinated IFR departures and reduced ARFF capabilities.

ASRS:1618904.n: Company charts and NOTAM's did not reflect an operational Control Tower/Ground Control/ATIS. We canceled IFR with Miami Center around 5,000 feet when we had the field in sight. I was making position reports on CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) and was contacted by Tower over CTAF with a frequency for Tower. We were approximately 15 miles out and performing a left 360 for separation at the time. Tower ask us to report established on final. When we were back on final they cleared us to land. On short final I noticed that the rotating beacon was on. After landing and taxiing in, I discovered that the Tower had been operational for the past two weeks. On flight after departing VFR and getting back into ACARS range we received the missing NOTAM for the first time, which reflected the information about the new Tower and that the ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting) had been downgraded. At this time we realized that the fire department on the field may not have been able to handle the amount of passengers our aircraft is able to carry.Lack of communication between the company and ATC. Previous [company] pilots not reporting changes over the past few weeks of flying into the airport.
ASRS:1618904.s: The pilot canceled IFR at 5,000 feet and landed VFR after discovering the tower was operational despite missing NOTAMs. The incident resulted from a lack of communication between the company and ATC, compounded by previous pilots failing to report the changes.

ASRS:1618916.n: Departed off Runway 34R and cleared to 9,000 feet. Upon reaching nearly 8,000 feet ATC advised us of traffic descending to 10,000 feet. We attempted to slow our ascent, but the aircraft had already entered 'altitude acquire' mode. At approximately 8,500 feet a TCAS Resolution Advisory (RA) was aurally and visually annunciated, with 'Level-Off' commanded. The Captain complied with the RA, but due to system lag and utilizing Flight Director TCAS RA cues, the airplane's climb was not fully arrested until about 8,700 feet. In order to comply with the TCAS RA Flight Director cues, the aircraft then descended to approximately 8,400 feet. Due to some confusion between interpretation of seemingly conflicting commands from the TCAS system ('Level-Off' aural vs. slightly descending FD cue), ATC was not notified until the conflict had already cleared. No unusual maneuvering was required, and ATC seemed to be surprised by the report of the RA.The TCAS Resolution Advisory system is outdated and does not contain logic for level-offs. Today's high-performance aircraft safely maintain steady higher-rate climbs and descents with programmed level-offs that the TCAS system is incapable of compensating for. This decades-old technology, which is designed as an added safety layer, is creating false positives in the already crowded modern airspace environment. These false positives then become a safety risk in and of themselves, due to deviations in ATC clearances that are required, and yet could create even more dangerous loss of separation. Secondary narrative contains no additonal information.
ASRS:1618916.s: The pilot reported a TCAS Resolution Advisory during climb to 9,000 feet after ATC advised of descending traffic. The crew attributed the event to outdated TCAS logic failing to account for modern aircraft climb rates, causing unnecessary altitude deviations and delayed ATC notification.

ASRS:1618935.n: Downwind vectoring off BRAUN Arrival for 13R. 2500 foot GPWS callout made on downwind, no approach clearance issued yet.
ASRS:1618935.s: The pilot reported a 2500-foot GPWS callout while being vectored on the downwind leg of the BRAUN Arrival for runway 13R. This occurred before an approach clearance had been issued.

ASRS:1618942.n: Just after top of climb upon reaching our [cruise] altitude of FL370 I heard a loud bang and a flash. When I looked up my forward window was completely shattered. We ran the QRH, called Dispatch and [Maintenance]. We decided our best option was to turn around and head back to ZZZ. After running the QRH, I handed the aircraft to my First Officer and had him fly the remainder of the flight due to my limited visibility. We notified ATC and [advised them] and told the controllers we wanted to turn back to ZZZ, slow down and descend to 10,000 in case of loss of pressurization. I believe we were still with Center.I briefed the flight attendants we had a mechanical situation and to prepare the cabin for landing and they had 25 minutes to touchdown and it would be a normal landing and we would be returning to a gate. I briefed the passengers and asked for [their patience] and cooperation to get the cabin ready. When ATC handed [us] off [to] Approach we told them we need XXL for landing, since our gate was located on the north side of the airport. I did not want to taxi across the airport with limited visibility.Despite [being] an emergency aircraft Approach was NOT helpful. They wanted us to land on Runway XY, which we replied that was not an option. They want to know why [we] couldn't accept XY and we told them operational. We landed on XXL, taxied to the gate without any further problems. The flight attendants did a great job. Captain's windshield cracked.
ASRS:1618942.s: The Captain reported a forward windshield shattering at FL370, causing limited visibility and necessitating a return to ZZZ. Despite Approach initially assigning Runway XY, the crew insisted on Runway XXL for gate access and landed safely.

ASRS:1618944.n: [I was] relief pilot at time of occurrence. Left autopilot and autothrottles engaged. The flight was in an auto-flight descent and on ATC vectors heading 155 to intercept Runway XXR LOC/ILS, descending to 2,000 feet in Flight Level Change 'FLCH', flaps 20 speed 190 knots. At LOC capture and in the turn descending through 2,100 feet the aircraft began an uncommanded climb and acceleration. At 210 knots the autopilot was disconnected and hand flown back to 2,000 with autothrottles engaged. Crew observed the airspeed now decreasing below 190 knots which alerted crew of potential autothrottle malfunction. Autothrottle was disconnected for remainder of the approach and landing. At no time did the crew observe a deviation off of the localizer course. Due to the unexplained altitude climb ATC broke the flight off the approach and vectored us around for an uneventful Runway XXR ILS approach and landing. Once the aircraft was stabilized at 2,000 feet left autopilot was reengaged until approximately 1200 feet AGL when autopilot was disconnected and a normal landing was accomplished. After we blocked in the auto-flight system malfunction was logged as a maintenance discrepancy.
ASRS:1618944.s: The relief pilot reported an uncommanded climb and acceleration during an ILS approach in auto-flight mode, prompting autopilot and autothrottle disconnection. ATC vectored the aircraft for a second approach, which was completed normally after the auto-flight malfunction was logged as a maintenance discrepancy.

ASRS:1618976.n: During push-back we got the EICAS 'ASD-B NOT AVAIL'. During the time we were referencing the QRH, the EICAS cleared on its own. I remembered getting the same exact EICAS a long time ago when the US military was testing GPS jamming equipment in the southwest US. So, when we got the EICAS and looked at QRH, I checked our NAV sensors in the MCDU, and I saw blank space for both GPS 1 and 2, which told we weren't getting a GPS position. After GPS 1 & 2 got positions again, the EICAS cleared and we started to taxi. Shortly into our taxi to 25R, we got the EICAS again. Now I wanted to pull over and call Maintenance Control. For reference the first instance occurred when we were in the gate area in LAX and the second occurred just as we made the turn onto TWY B off of C4. LAX Ground had us taxi B-C3-C hold short of C4 while we troubleshot. While on the phone with the company I was advised that the issue could be due to GPS jamming testing by [company name] or one of the other aerospace companies nearby. Ops Control suggested I move from my current position. I evaluated the situation and decided that I would try to give that plan a shot before returning to the gate for Maintenance. I intended to ask LAX ground that we taxi to the approach end of 25R and give the plane a few minutes to assess the situation and see if changing position impacted the GPS performance. A couple of points I want to add are, while I contacted Ops and Maintenance Control while we were on C short of C4, our GPS signal was so intermittent we got many EICAS messages for ADS-B NOT AVAIL. During that time, we asked Ground if anyone else was having the issue, and multiple AC reported no issue, though no one was close to our position at the time. During this time, I also referenced our SID, the SUMMR1, which had a note for 'DME/DME/IRU or GPS required'. Even if we were able to get the EICAS to clear and get a stable GPS signal prior to departure I did not want to assume I'd have it for the departure, so I contacted Clearance Delivery (CD) and advised them of our GPS issues and they decided to amend our clearance to the VTU8 and gave us a modified routing to ZZZ. Getting the clearance changed with CD took a while, Ground moved us up C to short of C6, and we waited there for over 10 minutes while we sorted out our clearance and checked our route. During that entire period while we were short of C6 we did not have any issues with our GPS signal, nor did we get any EICAS messages. That gave me some confidence that the company was correct, that some third party was testing GPS jamming equipment, and that we were in its effective radius. Now that the GPS was stable, and we had a modified clearance from ATC accounting for a potentially inoperative GPS, we took off and continued with normal operations. For the remainder of the flight we did not once lose GPS signal and had positions on GPS 1 and 2 the whole time. It seems there's a very good chance that a company is testing GPS jamming equipment in the vicinity of LAX. If this is true, I am very frustrated that this is occurring. Given the increasing use and reliance of GPS for RNAV and RNP navigation, GPS jamming, at best, causes an issue like mine that ends up just wasting time and fuel. At worse, this could potentially impact navigation performance in a critical phase of flight. Personally, I hope this kind of activity is banned within a given radius next to airports. At the very least a NOTAM, for which there was not one, would have helped me correctly and quickly identify the issue. When we started to push back, we got an EICAS message that said 'ASD-B NOT AVAIL'. As we opened the QRH and started reading through the procedure, the message went away on its own. We then checked the NAV sensors, which GPS 1 and 2 were blank, then as the EICAS message disappeared, the sensors came back. We then started to taxi, shortly after getting the message again (about C4). The Captain decided we needed to pull over and give Maintenance a call, so we contacted Ground and they told us B-C3-C hold short C4. Maintenance advised the CA that there could be some GPS jamming testing going on. So we tried to taxi towards the end of 25R to see if things would fix itself. We also asked Tower if any other planes were having any issues, they asked 3 others, who were not experiencing the same thing (though they were not near us). While we were stopped, we had the EICAS message come up again. The Captain (CA) decided to start looking at other departures that were not RNAV related, we ended up getting the VTU8 departure. While we grabbed clearance for our new departure, Ground moves us to C6, where we did not get the EICAS message again or issues with the sensors. After a while we decided the GPS was stable enough and we departed, having no further issues the entire flight.
ASRS:1618976.s: The crew experienced intermittent 'ASD-B NOT AVAIL' EICAS messages and GPS signal loss during push-back and taxi at LAX, likely caused by nearby GPS jamming tests. After moving to a different taxiway location and amending their clearance to the non-GPS VTU8 departure, the signal stabilized, allowing for a normal takeoff and flight.

ASRS:1618987.n: I departed as flying pilot, right seat, SIC (Second-in-Command). About an hour out from ZZZ1, the BRAKE FAIL CAS (Crew Alert System) message came on. We referenced the QRH for Brake Fail CAS message and realized that we needed to make a landing using the emergency brake system. I maintained control of the aircraft and the radios while the Captain called the company to confer on what to do and where to divert. He then called [the FBO] to coordinate ground handling then spoke with the passengers. I notified ATC that we needed to divert to ZZZ and that we were [requesting priority handling]. I also let them know that we needed to stop on runway and be towed off. At this point the Captain and I reviewed the QRH again and reviewed what needed to be done. We decided it would be better if he landed and operated the brakes, so we switched controls and I became the non-flying pilot. At this point I went back and briefed the passengers in greater detail on what to expect and how to evacuate. I used TEST as a basic guide. After reassuring them, I returned to my seat. We ran all appropriate checklists. We were vectored onto the GPS 27 and picked up the runway visually. We flew a standard stabilized approach, except the Captain got low on glideslope. I called for him to correct and he did. We touched down normally, and the Captain began using the emergency brake handle. He applied gradual, soft pressure, and we seemed to be slowing normally. Suddenly both tires blew and we rapidly came to a stop. There was a momentary pause, then I realized that we should run the emergency evacuation checklist, which we did to shut down and secured the plane. When I completed that checklist, I jumped out of my seat and went to main cabin door. I looked out window and saw no fire. I tentatively opened door to look out and saw a firefighter walking towards me. I opened door and walked down to talk to him and found everyone else followed me off the plane. The FBO took the passengers to the FBO, Operations towed the aircraft off the runway. We secured passenger bags and then secured aircraft.I thought we did a pretty good job. I would suggest in training this emergency to emphasize not to try to duck under glideslope to make an early touch down. I don't think blowing the tires could have been avoided, the Captain very slightly and gently pulled on the brake handle (I watched closely to see) and the tires blew regardless. Later, I heard a Maintenance Controller ask if we had tried the brake pedals first but we hadn't because that was not in the QRH checklist. We had briefed a lot about the approach and landing, and towing the airplane off the runway, but we didn't brief that we would do an evacuation checklist. We should have so it would have been a seamless transition from landing to securing the aircraft. I wish I had waited for an all clear signal from the firefighters before opening the door and I should have maintained better control over the passengers (they basically followed me out of the plane).
ASRS:1618987.s: The SIC reported a Brake Fail CAS message during cruise, leading to a diversion where the Captain landed using emergency brakes, causing both tires to blow out. The crew executed an evacuation checklist and secured the aircraft, though the SIC noted missed briefing opportunities and premature door opening.

ASRS:1618990.n: Got green laser on the left side of the aircraft in my left eye. Reported it to Tower and safely landed.
ASRS:1618990.s: The pilot reported a green laser strike on the left side of the aircraft affecting their left eye. The incident was reported to Tower, and the aircraft landed safely.

ASRS:1618993.n: After starting engines, BLEED 1 OFF and BLEED 2 OFF advisory messages were illuminated on EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System). The PIC and I acknowledged them, looked them up in the QRH, and discovered the uninformative 'Crew Awareness' line associated with them. We continued with the after start checklists and taxied to the runway. During my Before Takeoff flow, I noted the continued presence of the two messages on the EICAS, but did not consider them significant, as the AOM (Aircraft Operating Manual) only instructs pilots to consider yellow and red messages during the Right Pilot Before Takeoff flow. After takeoff, it became immediately evident that the airplane was not pressurizing properly. Further, upon activation, the anti-ice system was indicating inhibited when it should not have been. On the ECS (Environmental Control System) synoptic page, we noted that both PRSOV (Pressure regulating Shutoff Valve) valves were white and indicating OFF or CLOSED (no green line extending past the valve icon and the line in the valve icon perpendicular to the bleed air flow line).The PIC contacted the company and we arranged a diversion to ZZZ, where a suitable recovery could be made for our passengers. The flight progressed uneventfully, though unpressurized at 6,000 feet until our descent into ZZZ. As I began descending, a loud, vibratory swishing sound filled the entire airplane. It seemed constant no matter descent rate or airspeed. As we leveled at about 4,000 feet, the noise slowly faded away. It reminded me of the sounds that usually accompany a lavatory fill cap that has come loose, but a little bit louder and with a severe pressure bump in the ears.The QRH concerning white advisory messages in the Phenom is extremely uninformative and unhelpful. In any other airplane I have ever flown, advisory messages in the QRH are at least accompanied by a few things to consider or some explanation as to what is likely occurring within the given system. While it may be obvious that a BLEED OFF message means that the BLEED is off, this is not an entirely abnormal condition in the Phenom. Often, due to the air conditioning system on the ground, BLEED 1 and BLEED 2 cycle on and off automatically during ground operations. I have checked the EICAS many times during my Before Takeoff flow and noted BLEED OFF messages and thought nothing of them, as the PRSOVs always open and begin pressurizing the airplane and providing other bleed systems shortly after takeoff. The AOM normal Before Takeoff procedures prohibit a takeoff with yellow or red messages displayed on the EICAS unless associated with a known inoperative component, but this section says nothing about white messages or what to do if they are displayed.Even the MEL manual for BLEED OFF says vaguely, 'Not Applicable'(?). No dispatch conditions, no MEL procedure.Three of the most important reference manuals indicate that everything is fine with the BLEED system when very clearly everything is not fine. I wish that I could better explain the likely cause of this event, but I am still unsure of exactly why the system behaved as it did. With BLEED switches in the AUTO position, the system logic should have been controlling the BLEED valves, but in this instance, it failed to do so.
ASRS:1618993.s: The crew ignored BLEED 1 and 2 OFF advisory messages during preflight and takeoff, resulting in a Phenom failing to pressurize and inhibiting the anti-ice system. They diverted to ZZZ, flying unpressurized at 6,000 feet, attributing the failure to inadequate manual guidance and system logic not opening the PRSOVs.

ASRS:1619005.n: We were filed to DFW from ZZZ via …GUTZZ.BOOVE4. The Controller at ZZZ issued a 'cleared as filed' clearance. After takeoff, we received several shortcuts on the route, but were eventually cleared direct to GUTZZ. About 3 miles prior to EGADS intersection on the BOOVE4 Arrival, we were issued a 'descend via' the SOCKK3 Arrival. In the process of changing the arrival from the BOOVE4 to the SOCKK3, we overshot EGADS by about 3 miles on the 003 degree track. We managed to get the SOCKK3 Arrival programmed and sequenced direct to KIILO intersection. This took about 30 seconds to accomplish. We were queried by Center about our position being west of the 026 degree track. We explained we had been cleared as filed at ZZZ, which included the BOOVE4 Arrival and the SOCKK3 clearance caught us by surprise. She stated that she understood the problem. She cleared us direct to KILLO intersection (we were already going direct) and a descent to 10,000 feet. She later re-issued the SOCKK3 clearance and handed us off to Approach. Nothing else was said by the Controller regarding the course deviation.The Controller seemed busy and saturated with traffic due to the change in flow, she should have given us the new arrival clearance a lot sooner and not last minute. We could have asked for a vector and altitude while we uploaded the new arrival. I should have asked Center for a vector and an altitude since I was rapidly approaching a turn point in the Arrival with an explanation of our filed route versus clearance.
ASRS:1619005.s: Pilots flying from ZZZ to DFW overshot the EGADS intersection by three miles after a last-minute arrival change from BOOVE4 to SOCKK3 caused a 30-second delay in programming. The crew attributed the deviation to the controller's late clearance and traffic saturation, noting they should have requested vectors and altitude instead.

ASRS:1619157.n: At the time of the event, the FO (First Officer) was the pilot flying, we were cleared for the ILS approach, were on localizer, and were descending to 2400. Right before the FAF (Final Approach Fix), we both heard a 'pop.' The FO's attitude indicator was flagged, as was the pilot's attitude indicator. At first, we thought circuit breakers had popped, so we looked and saw none popped. A second later, we saw L AC BUS and R AC BUS illuminated, so that meant Inverter #1 had failed. The Captain took control of the aircraft, and we switched to the #2 Inverter. The attitude indicator indicated 'GYRO COMPUTER' for 5-10 seconds before those flags went away, and unfortunately, I drifted off of localizer and got to 3/4 deflection. As I was correcting, Tower called to inform us we were off course. I told them we had an inverter failure, switched to our 2nd inverter, and were correcting. They asked if we wanted vectors, and I said, 'I'm on localizer now, is that what you're showing?' She confirmed I was on localizer. We then landed.It was a system failure which caused me to drift off localizer. In the future, I will ask for vectors and go around. As for the plane, in my opinion, the root cause has not been identified, because this is the fourth Inverter #1 failure in about a month.
ASRS:1619157.s: During an ILS approach, a First Officer and Captain experienced an Inverter #1 failure that flagged both attitude indicators and caused the aircraft to drift off the localizer. The crew switched to Inverter #2, corrected the course, and landed safely, though the reporter noted this was the fourth such failure in a month.

ASRS:1619161.n: On takeoff at about 500 feet AGL, we had severe engine shutter. CHT (Cylinder Head Temperature) #2 & #3 redlined. I immediately took flight controls and queried ATC for a precautionary landing. Tower gave me runway XXR and I landed the aircraft. On the ground the CHT temps went back into the yellow. I began to taxi back to the ramp. When I was about to cross RWY XY/XZ, both went back to red. I asked ATC to taxi to the southeast ramp and shut down the engine. When I entered taxiway Uniform, CHT #3 went blank. I proceeded to shut down the aircraft. Contacted Dispatch and towed aircraft back without incident.
ASRS:1619161.s: The pilot experienced severe engine surging and redlined Cylinder Head Temperatures on cylinders 2 and 3 at 500 feet AGL during takeoff, prompting a precautionary landing. After temperatures spiked again while taxiing, the pilot shut down the aircraft on Taxiway Uniform and had it towed to the ramp.

ASRS:1619162.n: Upon initial climbout I [noticed] engine observation showed that the fuel flow was indicating 0 GPH (Gallons Per Hour) and all other fuel indications were blank, attempted to troubleshoot with no success. PFD (Primary Flight Display) then began to indicate 0% power while MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) showed a normal power setting. I contacted Departure and asked to return to [the departure airport]. Aircraft on takeoff was within the takeoff limitations but was above the landing limitation for weight. Having turned around so quickly the aircraft was still heavy, I implemented a soft field landing for touchdown due to heavy weight, contacted Maintenance and wrote up the plane.
ASRS:1619162.s: The pilot experienced fuel flow and power indication discrepancies during initial climbout, prompting a return to the departure airport. Due to the aircraft's weight exceeding landing limitations, the pilot executed a soft field landing and reported the issue to maintenance.

ASRS:1619175.n: Reno 9 Departure: The initial climb instructions for Runway 16L/16R state: 'Climb on heading 164 and IRNO Localizer south course.' This is not worded properly. It is impossible to fly a heading and a course at the same time. Runways 25 and 34L/R instructions do not have this error.
ASRS:1619175.s: A pilot reported that Reno 9 departure instructions for Runways 16L/16R incorrectly required climbing on both heading 164 and the IRNO Localizer south course simultaneously. The reporter stated this wording is impossible to fly, noting that instructions for Runways 25 and 34L/R do not contain this error.

ASRS:1619177.n: We were approaching PIT from the southwest with a plan for landing on Runway 28L. I was the pilot flying, and they kept us high for quite some time. Then as we were abeam the airport, cleared us to the final approach fix altitude, 3,000 feet (1875 feet AGL). They gave us a turn to 360 degrees that was a heading directly to the FAF at about three miles, but we were still apparently 1,000-1,500 feet above the FAF altitude and we were in Level Change. I had the speedbrakes deployed and flaps 5. They then gave us the heading of 320 degrees and cleared [us] for the visual approach. Still high at that point, I called for flaps 10, and armed VOR/LOC. I could tell that the intercept heading would not have us intercepting the final approach course until well inside the final approach fix. I then called for 'landing gear down;' and the Captain said 'I agree.' I had very good visuals with the runway and could see our rate of descent increasing. I knew we were still high, and going to intercept the glideslope first, so I armed approach.At that point, I was still on autopilot, and noticed my pitch mode in the FMA blanked out, and we were descending below glidepath, at approximately 1,600-1,700 feet AGL. The Captain said 'Where are you going?' at about the same time I heard a 'Caution Obstacle.' I immediately turned off autopilot and leveled and continued slowing, stowed the speed brakes, and called for flaps 15. I had good visual contact with the ground, and noticed we were approaching 1300 feet above field elevation, and close to glidepath. I called for 'Flaps 30, Before Landing Checklist;' and we completed the checklist and continued the approach to landing.I learned several important points. We should have gone around when we got the warning. I knew we'd have to do a [report on this incident], but did not initially realize we should have gone around in night conditions even if VMC. I should've also taken a turn back to the north to intercept final approach course instead of staying on the same heading prior to the visual clearance. I also think I was too worried about working the MCP and staying with the autopilot, rather than flying the aircraft and keeping my rate of descent under control.The Captain was supportive of my efforts to get back on glidepath, but reiterated that in night conditions, even if VMC, a 'Caution Obstacle' aural warning requires a go-around. I think I probably felt too confident with my flying skills, and accepted the short turn [to] final when I probably should have turned north to give myself more room to maneuver prior to intercepting the final approach course. It was the third month on the line for the First Officer. Approach Control gave us a vector to final for a visual approach that was inside the FAF. We were high on energy and I directed the First Officer to slow and get some drag out, which we started doing. I went heads down to find the Tower frequency and tune it in the radio. When I looked back up at the runway, I could see immediately we were low. At some point the First Officer had set zeros in the MCP altitude window and descended below the FAF altitude. First Officer asked for more flaps, and I instead directed a climb. He started to make the correction. At that time we got a 'Caution Obstacle' audio. I was already in the mode of directing a climb as well as power and configuration changes which had the desired result of correcting the flight path to a normal glidepath. The audio caution did not last long and shortly thereafter I realized that a go-around was the proper response but the correction to the flight path had already been made. At that point there was no need to go around as we were back on a proper path to the runway.
ASRS:1619177.s: During a night visual approach to PIT Runway 28L, the First Officer and Captain descended below glidepath after receiving a vector inside the FAF, triggering a "Caution Obstacle" warning. The crew leveled and corrected the flight path without executing a go-around, though the Captain later noted a go-around was required by procedure.

ASRS:1619190.n: On final, ATC advised windshear alert -30 knots at 200 feet, Company in front of us reported windshear and advised 'going around'.
